newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France's Juppe signals more cutbacks in 1998.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France's Juppe signals more cutbacks in 1998.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe fired the starting gun for another belt-tightening budget in 1998, releasing a letter on Thursday which told all ministries to cap spending for a second year running.

As the campaign for an early parliamentary election heated up, Juppe's office released a copy of the letter calling on all ministries to prepare further cutbacks to keep the lid on state spending, which he wants capped at 1996 levels.

Keeping spending at last year's levels in absolute terms means that state spending actually has to decrease to make up for the rise which would otherwise be implied by inflation, as it is trying to do this year.

"1997 will confirm France's ability to take part in European monetary union and a single currency from January 1, 1999. This decisive result for our country in European construction will be thanks to the clean-up of public finances pursued with vigour since 1995," Juppe says in the letter.
"You will draw up plans for savings which will ensure the maintenance of overall budget spending by the state in 1998 at the level of the 1997 budget finance law," he says.
The 1997 budget limits state spending this year at the same level as in 1996 -- 1,563 billion francs ($270 billion) -- which implies cuts to compensate for the automatic rise caused by inflation.

Juppe's letter, the traditional missive on budget goals for the following year, came at the same time as a reaffirmation by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis that France's finances for 1997 -- the decisive year for single currency qualification -- were in line with forecasts.

Arthuis said in an interview published in business daily Les Echos that there were no signs of slippage this year, stressing that tax revenue, including income from value added tax (VAT), was not below forecast.
"Nothing points to slippage in the state budget," he said. "Tax revenue, especially VAT, is not below forecasts."

Arthuis has repeatedly dismissed press speculation that this year's budget is under presuure, not because of problems with spending cuts, but because of possible tax revenue shortfalls and an overshoot on the forecast social security deficit.
"If in any case there were any nasty surprises, we would take sufficient measures to control spending levels," Arthuis said in a reiteration of the government line over past weeks.

"We have frozen 10 billion francs (of spending credits). If we had to go further, we would do it," he said. "I have strong hopes that we will also meet our goals on the social (security) accounts," he added.

Arthuis added there would be no "exceptional receipts" in the 1998 budget. Its 1997 arithmetic for limiting the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product includes 37.5 billion francs transferred from France Telecom, which knocks close to 0.5 percentage points off the key deficit figure.
He said the centre-right government wanted to go further on tax cuts and that this was taken into account in Juppe's letter.
"This control of spending excludes from now on any call on exceptional receipts," he said.

France's centre-right government is heading into a tough campaign battle with the main opposition Socialist party and keen to prove its economic track record to voters ahead of the two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1.

It got some help from figures issued on Monday which showed that industrial production, stripping out energy, agri-food and construction, rose 3.7 percent in February from the previous month, giving a year-on-year rise of 2.2 percent.
Economists read the data as a sign of economic pick-up but some said it was too early yet to have a reliable pattern.
The government is forecasting minimum 2.3 percent economic growth this year and vowing to cut the public deficit to three percent of GDP to qualify for a single currency.
But, at a time of record 12.8 percent unemployment, its push to keep finances in trim in following years means it is sure to have to impose more unpopular spending cuts in the 1998 budget.

The International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday France's budget deficit could hit 3.4 percent of GDP in 1998 and France would have to take extra steps to contain its deficit durably. ($ = 5.790 French Francs)
